# ==============================================================================
# DCTX TEMPLATE DEFINITION V1
# ==============================================================================
# This file defines how the LLM context is formatted.
# It consists of three sections: [VARIABLES], [PARTIALS], and [LAYOUT].
#
# SYNTAX GUIDE:
# - {{VAR_NAME}}      : Inserts a configuration variable defined in [VARIABLES].
# - {{{DATA_FIELD}}}  : Inserts dynamic data from the project (e.g., file content).
#
# ==============================================================================

[VARIABLES]
# --- 1. Syntactic Markers (Granular Control) ---
# Defines the exact characters used to wrap tags.
# Allows handling XML, HTML, or Custom formats safely.
start_marker_open  = "<"
start_marker_close = ">"
end_marker_open    = "</"
end_marker_close   = ">"

# --- 2. Semantic Marker Names ---
# Defines the keywords used inside the tags.
instr_marker         = "INSTRUCTIONS"
tree_start_marker    = "DIRECTORY_TREE"
tree_end_marker      = "DIRECTORY_TREE"
file_start_marker    = "FILE_CONTENT_START"
file_end_marker      = "FILE_CONTENT_END"

# --- 3. Attribute Keys ---
# Used inside tags to denote properties.
attr_id    = "ID"
attr_path  = "PATH"
attr_size  = "SIZE"
attr_lines = "LINES"
attr_mod   = "MOD"

# --- 4. Branding & Header Config ---
folder_denotation_marker = "DIRECTORY"

# --- 5. Instructions Block Text ---
# This text explains the format to the LLM. It references the variables above
# to ensure the instructions always match the actual format used.
# Use '\n' for new lines.
instructions_text = "1. Manifest: The {{start_marker_open}}{{tree_start_marker}}{{start_marker_close}} section lists all files.\n   - Each entry: [TYPE] RELATIVE_PATH ({{attr_id}}:UNIQUE_ID)\n   - TYPE is [D] for directory, [F] for file.\n2. Content Access: To read a specific file:\n   - Find its UNIQUE_ID from the directory tree.\n   - Search for the marker: {{start_marker_open}}{{file_start_marker}} {{attr_id}}="UNIQUE_ID"{{start_marker_close}}\n   - The content is between this marker and {{end_marker_open}}{{file_end_marker}} {{attr_id}}="UNIQUE_ID"{{end_marker_close}}"

# ==============================================================================
# [PARTIALS]
# Defines the look of repeated elements (Tree items and Files).
# ==============================================================================

# --- Tree Entry Partial ---
# Context: 'node' object
# Available Data: {{{node.type_char}}}, {{{node.path}}}, {{{node.id}}}, {{{node.mod}}}, {{{node.size}}}
# The default entry leaves {{{node.mod}}} and {{{node.size_part}}} out: a timestamp or a size changes on an edit or a touch
# and would break the byte-stable prefix of the page. Custom templates may still use {{attr_mod}}, {{{node.mod}}},
# {{{node.size}}} and {{{node.size_part}}}; `--tree-stamps=on` selects the stamped built-in (the 1.0.0 text).
[PARTIAL:TREE_ENTRY]
{{{node.type_char}}} {{{node.path}}} ({{attr_id}}:{{{node.id}}})

# --- File Block Partial ---
# Context: 'file' object
# Available Data: {{{file.id}}}, {{{file.path}}}, {{{file.lines}}}, {{{file.size}}}, {{{file.content}}}
[PARTIAL:FILE_BLOCK]
{{start_marker_open}}{{file_start_marker}} {{attr_id}}="{{{file.id}}}" {{attr_path}}="{{{file.path}}}" {{attr_lines}}="{{{file.lines}}}"{{start_marker_close}}
{{{file.content}}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{file_end_marker}} {{attr_id}}="{{{file.id}}}"{{end_marker_close}}

# ==============================================================================
# [LAYOUT]
# The master structure of the final output file.
# Note: The Version Header (e.g. [DCTX_SNAPSHOT_V1]) is hardcoded in the binary
# and NOT included here.
# ==============================================================================
[LAYOUT]
[{{folder_denotation_marker}}:{{{project}}}]

{{start_marker_open}}{{instr_marker}}{{start_marker_close}}
{{instructions_text}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{instr_marker}}{{end_marker_close}}

{{start_marker_open}}{{tree_start_marker}}{{start_marker_close}}
{{{comp.tree}}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{tree_end_marker}}{{end_marker_close}}

{{{comp.files}}}

</FILE_CONTENT_END ID="F011">

<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 -->
<!-- SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Eris Margeta -->
# ADR-003: Extensible Templating System (DTS) & Compilation Strategy

**Status:** current — architectural principle retained; historical examples describe their original release.

For shipped behavior and limitations, see the [README](../README.md), [testing guide](TESTING.md) and [specification](SPEC.md).
**Date:** 2026-01-08
**Author:** dctx Team
**Context:** Users require granular control over the output format to support various AI models. The system must maintain high performance (avoiding expensive parsing on every run) and ensure robustness (instructions matching output).

## 1. Decision: Explicit Marker Definition
To ensure future compatibility with non-HTML-like syntax, the templating language separates "Opening" and "Closing" logic for tags into four distinct definitions:
*   `start_marker_open` (Default: `<`)
*   `start_marker_close` (Default: `>`)
*   `end_marker_open` (Default: `</`)
*   `end_marker_close` (Default: `>`)

This allows users to redefine tags completely, e.g., to `[SECTION]` ... `[/SECTION]` or `{{#SECTION}}` ... `{{/SECTION}}`.

## 2. Decision: "Ahead-of-Time" (AOT) Template Compilation
Parsing text templates, validating variable references, and checking for cycles is expensive. We will **not** do this during the standard `dctx` runtime.

### The "Baked-In" Default
The default template (defined in the ADR) is parsed at **Rust Compile Time** (or hardcoded as a static struct). This ensures `dctx` runs with zero parsing overhead out-of-the-box.

### User Custom Templates
Users can edit templates in `~/.config/dctx/templates/`. However, `dctx` does not read these text files directly during snapshot generation.
*   **Action:** User edits `.dctx_template` file.
*   **Command:** User runs `dctx template build <path>`.
*   **Process:**
    1.  `dctx` parses the text file.
    2.  Validates syntax and variable references.
    3.  Serializes the parsed structure into an optimized binary format (e.g., `bincode`).
    4.  Saves the result to `~/.cache/dctx/templates/user_custom.bin`.
*   **Runtime:** When `dctx` runs, if configured to use a custom template, it loads this pre-validated binary directly into memory.

## 3. Decision: Two-Pass Rendering Engine
The rendering engine operates in two distinct passes to separate Configuration from Data.

*   **Pass 1 (Config Resolution):** Occurs during the "Template Build" phase. Resolves all `{{VAR}}` placeholders within the `[VARIABLES]` section.
*   **Pass 2 (Data Injection):** Occurs during runtime. Injects `{{{DATA}}}` into the pre-compiled Partial structures (`[PARTIALS]` section) and assembles the `[LAYOUT]`.

## 4. Template File Structure
The file format uses a custom INI-like syntax with three specific sections:
1.  **[VARIABLES]:** Key-Value pairs for static strings.
2.  **[PARTIALS]:** Definitions for repeated elements (`TREE_ENTRY`, `FILE_BLOCK`).
3.  **[LAYOUT]:** The global document structure.

## 5. Available Data Variables (Runtime)
These variables are populated by the Rust core:
*   `{{{node.id}}}`: Optimized incremental ID (e.g., 1, 2, 10).
*   `{{{node.path}}}`: Relative path.
*   `{{{node.type_char}}}`: `[D]` or `[F]`.
*   `{{{node.mod}}}`: Unix timestamp in milliseconds. Available to custom templates. The built-in default template does not print it since 1.0.1, because a timestamp changes on a bare `touch` and breaks the byte-stable prefix of the page; `--tree-stamps=on` selects the built-in stamped template (the 1.0.0 text, `MOD:` and `SIZE:` on every tree line, `MOD` in the instructions). The default entry also leaves out `{{{node.size_part}}}`, since a size changes on every ordinary edit; `{{{node.size}}}` and `{{{node.size_part}}}` stay available to custom templates.
*   `{{{node.size}}}`: File size in bytes.
*   `{{{file.lines}}}`: Line count of the file.
*   `{{{file.content}}}`: Actual file content.



6. TEMPLATE DEFINITION V1:

```text
# ==============================================================================
# DCTX TEMPLATE DEFINITION V1
# ==============================================================================
# This file defines how the LLM context is formatted.
# It consists of three sections: [VARIABLES], [PARTIALS], and [LAYOUT].
#
# SYNTAX GUIDE:
# - {{VAR_NAME}}      : Inserts a configuration variable defined in [VARIABLES].
# - {{{DATA_FIELD}}}  : Inserts dynamic data from the project (e.g., file content).
#
# ==============================================================================

[VARIABLES]
# --- 1. Syntactic Markers (Granular Control) ---
# Defines the exact characters used to wrap tags.
# Allows handling XML, HTML, or Custom formats safely.
start_marker_open  = "<"
start_marker_close = ">"
end_marker_open    = "</"
end_marker_close   = ">"

# --- 2. Semantic Marker Names ---
# Defines the keywords used inside the tags.
instr_marker         = "INSTRUCTIONS"
tree_start_marker    = "DIRECTORY_TREE"
tree_end_marker      = "DIRECTORY_TREE"
file_start_marker    = "FILE_CONTENT_START"
file_end_marker      = "FILE_CONTENT_END"

# --- 3. Attribute Keys ---
# Used inside tags to denote properties.
attr_id    = "ID"
attr_path  = "PATH"
attr_size  = "SIZE"
attr_lines = "LINES"
attr_mod   = "MOD"

# --- 4. Instructions Block Text ---
# This text explains the format to the LLM. It references the variables above
# to ensure the instructions always match the actual format used.
# Use '\n' for new lines.
instructions_text = "1. Manifest: The {{start_marker_open}}{{tree_start_marker}}{{start_marker_close}} section lists all files.\n   - Each entry: [TYPE] RELATIVE_PATH ({{attr_id}}:UNIQUE_ID)\n   - TYPE is [D] for directory, [F] for file.\n2. Content Access: To read a specific file:\n   - Find its UNIQUE_ID from the directory tree.\n   - Search for the marker: {{start_marker_open}}{{file_start_marker}} {{attr_id}}=\"UNIQUE_ID\"{{start_marker_close}}\n   - The content is between this marker and {{end_marker_open}}{{file_end_marker}} {{attr_id}}=\"UNIQUE_ID\"{{end_marker_close}}"

# ==============================================================================
# [PARTIALS]
# Defines the look of repeated elements (Tree items and Files).
# ==============================================================================

# --- Tree Entry Partial ---
# Context: 'node' object
# Available Data: {{{node.type_char}}}, {{{node.path}}}, {{{node.id}}}, {{{node.mod}}}, {{{node.size}}}
# The default entry leaves {{{node.mod}}} and {{{node.size_part}}} out (1.0.1); a custom template may add `, {{attr_mod}}:{{{node.mod}}}{{{node.size_part}}}`.
[PARTIAL:TREE_ENTRY]
{{{node.type_char}}} {{{node.path}}} ({{attr_id}}:{{{node.id}}})

# --- File Block Partial ---
# Context: 'file' object
# Available Data: {{{file.id}}}, {{{file.path}}}, {{{file.lines}}}, {{{file.size}}}, {{{file.content}}}
[PARTIAL:FILE_BLOCK]
{{start_marker_open}}{{file_start_marker}} {{attr_id}}="{{{file.id}}}" {{attr_path}}="{{{file.path}}}" {{attr_size}}="{{{file.size}}}" {{attr_lines}}="{{{file.lines}}}"{{start_marker_close}}
{{{file.content}}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{file_end_marker}} {{attr_id}}="{{{file.id}}}"{{end_marker_close}}

# ==============================================================================
# [LAYOUT]
# The master structure of the final output file.
# Note: The Version Header (e.g. [DCTX_SNAPSHOT_V1]) is hardcoded in the binary
# and NOT included here.
# ==============================================================================
[LAYOUT]
{{start_marker_open}}{{instr_marker}}{{start_marker_close}}
{{instructions_text}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{instr_marker}}{{end_marker_close}}

{{start_marker_open}}{{tree_start_marker}}{{start_marker_close}}
{{{comp.tree}}}
{{end_marker_open}}{{tree_end_marker}}{{end_marker_close}}

{{{comp.files}}}
```

<!-- SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Eris Margeta -->
# ADR-014: Privacy Guarantees & Ignore Semantics

**Status:** current — architectural principle retained; historical examples describe their original release.

For shipped behavior and limitations, see the [README](../README.md), [testing guide](TESTING.md) and [specification](SPEC.md). Earlier “formally proven” wording refers to historical tests; tests and defense layers do not constitute a formal proof of all implementations.
**Date:** 2026-02-02
**Approved:** 2026-02-02
**Implemented:** 2026-02-02 (WO-050 through WO-054)
**Deciders:** Operator, AI Assistant
**Context:** Phase 10.6 - Safety-Critical Privacy & Performance Audit

---

## Context and Problem Statement

Users trust `dctx` with their entire codebases, including sensitive files like `.env`, `.git/`, API keys, credentials, and proprietary source code. Our ignore and omit systems were implemented primarily for output cleanliness and token efficiency, but we have not formally guaranteed that ignored files are **NEVER** read into memory.

**Critical Questions:**
1. Are ignored files (`.env`, credentials) ever read into memory?
2. Does the `--debug-ignored` flag compromise privacy?
3. What is the semantic difference between IGNORE and OMIT?
4. Can template variables accidentally trigger file reads on ignored files?
5. Do we recurse into ignored folders (performance impact)?

**Risk:** Without formal privacy guarantees, users cannot trust `dctx` with sensitive codebases. A single accidental file read could expose credentials, leak proprietary code, or violate security policies.

---

## Decision Drivers

* **Privacy First:** Ignored files must NEVER be read, regardless of flags or configuration
* **Performance:** Ignored folders must be skipped entirely (no recursion)
* **Semantic Clarity:** IGNORE vs OMIT must have clear, enforced meanings
* **Debug Transparency:** Users must be able to verify their ignore rules work correctly
* **Template Safety:** Custom templates must not accidentally trigger I/O on ignored files
* **Zero Trust:** Assume users handle classified/sensitive information

---

## Considered Options

### Option 1: Status Quo (No Formal Guarantees)
* **Pro:** No code changes required
* **Pro:** Current behavior is already safe (but undocumented)
* **Con:** No formal verification or tests
* **Con:** Users cannot trust the system
* **Con:** Template variables could be unsafe in the future
* **Verdict:** [no] Rejected - Privacy must be provable, not assumed

### Option 2: Full Privacy Audit + Formal Guarantees (SELECTED)
* **Pro:** Provable privacy through code analysis and tests
* **Pro:** Clear semantic distinction between IGNORE and OMIT
* **Pro:** Template variable safety system prevents accidental reads
* **Pro:** Performance optimizations (skip ignored folders)
* **Pro:** Debug mode that doesn't compromise privacy
* **Con:** Requires implementation work (2-3 hours)
* **Verdict:** [yes] **SELECTED** - Only acceptable solution for sensitive codebases

### Option 3: Encryption-Based Approach
* **Pro:** Could encrypt ignored file contents in memory
* **Con:** Massive complexity, performance overhead
* **Con:** Doesn't solve the problem (still reading files)
* **Verdict:** [no] Rejected - Overengineered, doesn't address root issue

---

## Decision Outcome

**Chosen Option:** Option 2 - Full Privacy Audit + Formal Guarantees

We will implement a three-tier rule system with formal privacy guarantees:

---

## Rule System Definition

| Rule Type | Directory Tree Visibility | File Content Section | Recurse into Folders? | Read File into Memory? |
|-----------|---------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|------------------------|
| **IGNORE** (default) | [no] Hidden | [no] Hidden | [no] NO (skip entirely) | [no] **NEVER** |
| **IGNORE** (`--debug-ignored`) | [yes] Shown with `[IGNORED]` marker | [no] Hidden | [yes] YES (for diagnostics) | [no] **NEVER** |
| **OMIT** (always) | [yes] Shown (normal) | [warning] `[Content omitted by pattern rules]` | [yes] YES | [no] **NEVER** |

---

## Semantic Definitions

### IGNORE
**Meaning:** "This file/folder does not exist for our purposes."

**Use Cases:**
- `.git/` - Version control internals
- `node_modules/`, `target/`, `__pycache__/` - Build artifacts
- `.env`, `.secrets` - Credentials and sensitive configuration
- `*.log`, `*.tmp` - Temporary files

**Behavior:**
- Default: Not visible in tree, not in content, folder not recursed
- Debug Mode: Visible in tree with `[IGNORED]` marker, folder recursed, but files never read
- Configuration: `.dctxignore` (project) or `~/.config/dctx/ignore` (global)

### OMIT
**Meaning:** "This file exists and is relevant to the project structure, but we don't care about its contents."

**Use Cases:**
- `package-lock.json`, `Cargo.lock` - Lockfiles (structure matters, content doesn't)
- `*.svg` - Image files (relevant to project, but binary/verbose)
- `go.sum`, `yarn.lock` - Dependency checksums

**Behavior:**
- Always visible in directory tree (with metadata)
- Content section shows: `[Content omitted by pattern rules]`
- File is listed but never read into memory

### Debug Mode (`--debug-ignored`)
**Purpose:** Allow users to verify their ignore rules are working correctly.

**Behavior:**
- Temporarily treats IGNORE rules as OMIT rules for visibility
- Shows ignored files/folders in directory tree with `[IGNORED]` marker
- Recurses into ignored folders to show structure
- **CRITICAL:** Files are still NEVER read into memory
- Grayed-out metadata: SIZE from `stat()` only, never from content reading
- No LINES count (would require reading file)

### SENSITIVE (strict deny, v1)
**Meaning:** "This file holds credentials. No dctx command ever reads, hashes, indexes or prints its bytes."

**Shapes** (final path component, ASCII case-insensitive; the single list is
`dctx_core::filter::is_secret_shaped_name`):
- env files: `.env`, `.env.*`, `*.env`, `.envrc`
- keys, certificates and keystores: `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore`
- SSH private keys: `id_rsa`, `id_dsa`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_ed25519`, and those names with a `_`/`-` suffix
  without a dot (`id_rsa_deploy`); `id_rsa.pub` is not matched
- credentials: `credentials`, `credentials.<data>`, `*.credentials.json`, `secrets.<data>`
  (data = `json`, `yaml`, `yml`, `toml`, `ini`, `xml`); `credentials.py` and `secrets.rs` stay ordinary source
- token files: `.netrc`, `_netrc`, `.npmrc`, `.pypirc`, `.pgpass`, `.htpasswd`, `.git-credentials`

**Behavior:**
- The file stays listed by name (pack tree, map inventory) with its content omitted, and is never read.
- Applies whether or not the file is git-tracked, to every surface: `pack` (all view filters, including
  `--include`, `--ext`, `--hidden` and `--debug-ignored`), every `dctx map` verb (map, find, read, explain,
  skeleton, grep, neighbors, hubs, path, export; by stable id or by raw path; with or without `--in`) and the
  `dctx mcp` tools, which run the same code path.
- Enforced in the map policy (`PolicyView::decide`), again before any map read (`Session::read_verified`),
  in map grep, in the pack scan (`dctx-pack` snapshot) and in the `dctx-map-query` source adapter.
- **No override.** v1 has no `--allow-sensitive` flag, and repository or global rule files cannot
  re-include these shapes. dctx decides by name only; it does not scan contents, so a secret pasted into an
  ordinary source file is not detected.

**Verification:** `crates/dctx/tests/map_sensitive_files.rs`, the unit tests next to
`is_secret_shaped_name`, `PolicyView::decide` and the pack scan, and the end-to-end check
`<repo>/scripts/checks/V1-1.zsh` (a git-tracked fixture with one canary per shape, run against every command).

### `.git` (hard guard, v1)
Any path with a `.git` segment, at any depth, is excluded by `PolicyView::decide` before the rule layers are
consulted, so `!.git/`, `!.g*/` or `!nested/.git/**` in `.gitignore` or `.dctxignore` cannot re-include it: the
map verbs never list or read it, and `Session::read_verified` refuses it too. `pack` excludes it as well
(`dctx-pack` snapshot); only `--debug-ignored` still lists it by name, never reading it. Tests:
`git_negations_never_list_or_read_git` in `crates/dctx/tests/git_and_symlink_privacy.rs` and in the pack snapshot.

### Symlinks (v1)
`dctx::FsSource` never follows a symlink: a symlinked final component is refused before the open, and the open
itself uses `O_NOFOLLOW` (raw platform values; crates/dctx has no `libc` dependency), so a symlink swapped in after
the stat is refused by the kernel; the opened handle must be a regular file. A symlinked intermediate directory is
refused for listings and reads. Tests: `crates/dctx/src/adapters/fs.rs` and `crates/dctx/tests/git_and_symlink_privacy.rs`.

### `DCTX_INDEX_IGNORED=1`
This environment switch (dctx-cli `host::project_rules`) makes `pack` and the map verbs ignore every ignore file
(global ignore, `.gitignore`, nested `.gitignore`, `.dctxignore`); omit files and the built-in rules still load.
It does not touch the SENSITIVE deny, the `.git` guard or the symlink rules above: those do not come from rule
files. `<repo>/scripts/checks/V1-1.zsh` reruns its canary checks with the switch set.

---

## Privacy Guarantees (Formal)

### Guarantee 1: Ignored Files Never Enter Read Queue [yes]
**Assertion:** Files matching ignore rules are excluded at tree construction time (`walker.rs:136-146`) via `should_ignore_item()` check. They never appear in the `DirContextTreeNode` tree, therefore never collected by `collect_file_paths()`, therefore never read by `populate_file_contents_parallel()`.

**Verification:** [yes] PROVEN
- [yes] Static code analysis completed (WO-052)
- [yes] Unit test: `test_collect_file_paths_skips_ignored` - ignored file never in read queue
- [yes] Unit test: `test_collect_file_paths_skips_ignored_subtree` - entire subtrees skipped
- [yes] Privacy guarantee formally proven through test chain

### Guarantee 2: Ignored Folders Skip Recursion
**Assertion:** When a folder matches ignore rules, `walk_recursive()` uses `continue` (walker.rs:146) to skip the item entirely. The function is never called recursively on that folder's children.

**Verification:**
- Performance benchmark: 500MB `node_modules/` should take < 100ms to skip
- Without ignore: Same folder would take 5-10 seconds to scan
- Debug mode exception: Recurses but still never reads files

### Guarantee 3: Debug Mode Does Not Compromise Privacy [yes]
**Assertion:** When `--debug-ignored` is active, the system recurses into ignored folders and shows them in the tree, but the files are marked with `is_ignored: true` flag. The `populate_file_contents_parallel()` function respects this flag and never calls `fs::read()` on ignored files.

**Verification:** [yes] PROVEN
- [yes] Test: `test_ignored_files_shown_with_marker` - `.env` appears in tree with [IGNORED]
- [yes] Test: `test_ignored_files_never_have_content` - no content blocks for ignored files
- [yes] Test: `test_collect_file_paths_skips_ignored` - ignored files never enter read queue
- [yes] Privacy preserved even in debug mode (WO-051, WO-052, WO-053)

### Guarantee 4: Template Variables Cannot Trigger Unsafe Reads [yes]
**Assertion:** Template variables are classified by I/O requirement:
- **Metadata-Only:** `{{{file_id}}}`, `{{{file_path}}}`, `{{{file_size}}}`, `{{{mod}}}` (safe - from `stat()`)
- **Content-Requiring:** `{{{lines}}}`, `{{{content_preview}}}` (unsafe - requires `fs::read()`)

For ignored/omitted files, content-requiring variables are never resolved due to `!node.is_ignored` guard preventing content block rendering.

**Verification:** [yes] PROVEN
- [yes] Test: `test_template_variable_safety_for_ignored_files` with 6 comprehensive assertions (WO-054)
- [yes] Documentation: Module-level safety documentation in llm_formatter.rs
- [yes] Documentation: Template Variable Safety section in DEVELOPER-GUIDE.md
- [yes] Multi-layer defense prevents any code path from triggering reads on ignored files

---

## Performance Characteristics

### Ignored Folder Skip (Primary Optimization)
**Scenario:** Project with 500MB `node_modules/` (50,000 files)

| Mode | Behavior | Time | `fs::read()` Calls |
|------|----------|------|-------------------|
| Default | Skip entire folder | < 100ms | 0 |
| Without ignore | Scan all 50k files | 5-10 sec | 50,000 |
| Debug mode | Recurse but don't read | < 500ms | 0 |

**Performance Gain:** 50-100x faster for large ignored folders.

### Omit Pattern Performance
**Scenario:** Lockfiles in monorepo (20 files, 10MB each)

| Mode | Behavior | Time | Memory |
|------|----------|------|--------|
| Include all | Read all lockfiles | ~200ms | 200MB |
| Omit lockfiles | Show in tree, skip content | ~10ms | 2MB |

**Performance Gain:** 20x faster, 100x less memory.

---

## Consequences

### Positive
[yes] **Provable Privacy:** Users can verify ignored files are never read
[yes] **Performance Boost:** 50-100x faster for projects with large ignored folders
[yes] **Semantic Clarity:** IGNORE vs OMIT distinction is clear and enforced
[yes] **Debug Transparency:** Users can verify ignore rules without compromising privacy
[yes] **Template Safety:** Custom templates cannot accidentally leak ignored file contents
[yes] **Trust:** Enterprise users can confidently use `dctx` on classified codebases

### Neutral
[settings] **Implementation Cost:** 2-3 hours of development work
[settings] **Test Overhead:** 4 new privacy tests, 2 performance benchmarks
[settings] **Documentation:** ADR, README security section, developer guide updates

### Negative
[no] **API Change:** `walk_recursive()` signature changes (internal API only)
[no] **Binary Size:** +1-2KB for additional logic (negligible)
[no] **Complexity:** Template variable classification system adds minor complexity

# ADR-018: Language Coverage

**Status:** superseded — historical design and implementation record.

The original 13-family scope below is superseded by the [current language registry table](../README.md#language-tiers); confidence and completion principles remain relevant.

## Context

### The Problem

Map facts need explicit coverage and completion claims across source/configuration languages; precision is separate from edge confidence (`crates/dctx-map-model/src/domain/precision.rs`).

### Root Cause Analysis

Structural extraction is not a full grammar claim, and incomplete extraction must not silently become complete facts (`crates/dctx-map-model/src/domain/precision.rs`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`).

## Decision

Use pure structural extraction for 13 families: Rust, JavaScript/TypeScript, Markdown, Python, Go, Java, C/C++, configuration (JSON/TOML/YAML), C#, Kotlin, Ruby, PHP and Swift (`crates/dctx/src/index/extract.rs`, `docs/CRATE-MAP.md`).

The facade's default profile uses hand-written extraction, including line-oriented Rust and the first-party Markdown extractor. **Qualification:** `dctx-lex-rust` itself uses `syn`; it is optional behind facade `syntax-rust`, so “13 hand-written lexers” is not a claim about every lexer crate or map-parse Rust implementation (`crates/dctx/src/index/extract.rs`, `crates/dctx/Cargo.toml`, `crates/dctx-lex-rust/src/lib.rs`).

Keep one shared facade dispatch and fact-to-symbol conversion in `crates/dctx/src/index/lex_dispatch.rs`; Rust and Markdown retain specialized entry paths in `crates/dctx/src/index/extract.rs`.

Carry coverage (`syntax`, `structural`, `opaque`), completion (`complete`, `partial`, `refused`) and bounded parser identity separately from confidence (`crates/dctx-map-model/src/domain/precision.rs`).

## Implementation

### Phase 1: Pure Lexers and Facade Projection

The shared dispatch converts nodes without reading source or retaining bodies. New language branches expose only complete extraction; JavaScript/TypeScript preserve their existing partial-fact projection (`crates/dctx/src/index/lex_dispatch.rs`).

The facade rejects NUL/non-UTF-8 symbol extraction and assigns stable ids and containment after extraction (`crates/dctx/src/index/extract.rs`).

### Phase 2: Map-parse Adapters

`PureParser` dispatches the language adapters over caller-provided bytes; partial/diagnostic extraction is refused as `ParseError::Syntax`, and unknown languages have a module-only fallback (`crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`).

Shared fact assembly records file precision and finalizes source-ordered facts with duplicate-id handling (`crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/facts.rs`).

### Phase 3: Store Invariants Gate

The parser gate checks file ownership, unique/kind-correct ids, source-bounded spans, valid confidence/kind combinations, existing edge endpoints and containment reachability. It also simulates query insertion of Place/Package nodes to catch duplicate ids (`crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/lexers.rs`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/fuzz_all.rs`).

### Phase 4: Fuzz Gate

Seeded bounded property tests exercise arbitrary bytes, Unicode, malformed inputs, deterministic results, successful-result store invariants and fixture prefixes without executing source (`crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/fuzz_all.rs`).

## Results

The gate source defines successful fixture controls as well as refusal/robustness cases; this record asserts test obligations, not a new passing execution (`crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/lexers.rs`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/fuzz_all.rs`).

## Trade-offs

### Benefits

Structural facts can be produced without a default tree-sitter runtime, with explicit precision and conservative abstention (`crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`, `crates/dctx/src/index/lex_dispatch.rs`).

### Costs

The facade's structural Rust profile and optional syn path differ; the shared facade dispatch also deliberately differs from PureParser on JavaScript partial facts (`crates/dctx/src/index/extract.rs`, `crates/dctx/src/index/lex_dispatch.rs`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`).

## Alternatives Considered

The earlier spec proposed tree-sitter as the parser dependency. Current adapters retain it only behind `syntax-tree-sitter` as an optional oracle; languages without an included grammar use pure adapters even in that oracle (`docs/SPEC-MAP-MODE.md`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`).

## References

Inventory: `docs/CRATE-MAP.md`; facade: `crates/dctx/src/index/lex_dispatch.rs`; adapters: `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`; robustness: `crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/fuzz_all.rs`.

## Lessons Learned

Language family count, structural coverage, grammar completeness and edge confidence are distinct claims; the Rust implementation qualification must remain visible (`docs/CRATE-MAP.md`, `crates/dctx-map-model/src/domain/precision.rs`, `crates/dctx-lex-rust/src/lib.rs`).

## Future Work

Keep tree-sitter optional and preserve precision/refusal and store-invariant gates when extending adapters; optional oracle coverage is limited to its included grammars (`crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs`, `crates/dctx-map-parse/tests/fuzz_all.rs`).

</FILE_CONTENT_END ID="F016">

# dctx measurement: grep plus file reads first

The baseline for choosing dctx is **grep plus reading files**. Count the whole
agent session before claiming a cost saving. Output bytes and estimated output
tokens measure only the returned context; they exclude startup instructions,
tool descriptions, conversation replay, model output and provider cache effects.

## Grep plus file reads

The [11 November whole-session benchmark](BENCHMARK-20261111.md) measured grep plus reads against dctx CLI and MCP: CLI median total tokens -5.01 %; the pre-registered 25 % savings rule was not met.
Official strict citation recall medians (A/B/C): 10.10 % / 14.46 % / 13.41 %; diagnostic file-level recall: 53.77 % / 71.70 % / 76.42 %. The claim is accuracy and bounded context, not token savings.
On this corpus and model dctx did not save 25 % tokens; MCP cost +6.8 % tokens and +30 % wall time. The linked report gives median [min, max], methods and limitations; corpus and raw answers are private.

## Secondary historical evidence: other-tool protocols

Everything below retains the October/November research record, including its
older limitations and plans. These other-tool comparisons are historical notes,
not the product's headline baseline or a recommendation between tools. All
"tokens" in these tables mean estimated **tool stdout tokens**, calculated as
`ceil(stdout_bytes / 3.5)`, never whole-session tokens. Task scores are fact
coverage in raw outputs without a model, not agent completion rates.

One command, same host, same corpora, same CPU set, no network, pinned versions. Raw aggregate, headline tables
and the harness are in [`research/bench-3way-20261030/`](research/bench-3way-20261030/); the current goals are in the [specification](SPEC.md). Where another tool wins, the tables say so.

- **dctx**: `main` at `ac8408c` (the following commit only changes `CHANGELOG.md`), release build,
  sha256 `82bd48760932305748a00d2b32901c667af948f602822b9816cc5c545de7ebbc`.
  Baseline for "before" columns: `main` at `4660f6d`, the state before this night's work.
- **Trail-Code** `@trailhq/trail-code` 0.28.0 from npm, `trail build .` (no `--deep`, no `--lsp`).
- **graphify** `graphifyy` 0.9.97 from PyPI, LLM-free code path only (`extract --code-only`,
  `GRAPHIFY_BACKEND=none`). Its LLM pass over docs, PDFs and images was **not** run, and nothing here measures it.

## Historical three-way summary

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Task-level questions, October protocol (70 questions) | **Run 7: dctx 140 of 140, Trail-Code 122, graphify 96**, with dctx using 29.3k tokens against Trail-Code's 88.9k and graphify's 197k. See "Run 7" below. |
| Callers (depth 1) against a tool-independent gold set, 80 targets on 4 corpora | **Run 5: dctx P 0.995 / R 0.851 (first page), R 0.968 following 5 pages.** Run 1 below: dctx P 0.993 / R 0.461 (first page), P 0.995 / R 0.706 following up to 5 pages. Trail-Code P 0.986 / R 0.436, graphify P 0.989 / R 0.196. Per corpus, Trail-Code wins ripgrep and trailcode, and dctx wins flask and pocketbase. Before tonight dctx recall was 0. |
| Cold index | **dctx fastest on all 6 corpora**: 0.16–1.16 s against 1.17–58.3 s for Trail-Code and 4.5–59 s for graphify. Peak RSS 19–90 MB against 121–1,020 MB and 74–394 MB. |
| Warm queries (median of 5, including process start) | **dctx fastest** on search, callers and skeleton everywhere: 44–226 ms against 0.98–1.9 s for Trail-Code and 0.38–1.4 s for graphify. graphify's overview is a 7 ms read of a pre-written file. |
| Answer size | dctx `map hubs` gives the smallest overview on 4 of 6 corpora (Trail-Code on trailcode and docs) (30–652 tokens; Trail-Code 18–2,538; graphify 3,827–11,591). graphify gives the smallest callers and skeleton answers. dctx's skeleton is the largest of the three on ripgrep (1,784 tokens). Before tonight dctx's only overview was a 0.45–2.6 M-token `pack`. |
| Cache-friendliness | dctx and Trail-Code tie. Both are byte-identical across runs, and after an unrelated edit only the overview changes. graphify changed find, skeleton and overview after `update`, and 1 of 6 ripgrep queries was not deterministic. |
| Network | dctx and graphify made 0 socket attempts in every variant. Trail-Code made 49 blocked connect attempts when `DO_NOT_TRACK` is unset, and 0 with it set. |
| Language coverage, mixed corpus (10 languages) | **Symbols: dctx 10 of 10, Trail-Code 7, graphify 5.** **Call edges, run 3: dctx 10 of 10, Trail-Code 7, graphify 5** (run 1: dctx 0). dctx's new outline tier is symbols only, labelled `guess`. Terraform and SQL get symbols only from dctx. |
| Plain-text docs (.md/.rst/.txt/.adoc corpus) | dctx indexes the corpus into headed sections (0.18 s). graphify's code-only mode produced no index, and Trail-Code indexes no doc nodes. |
| Privacy canary (git-tracked `.env` files) | Run 3: **clean for all three tools** after sensitive-file read protection landed. In run 1, `pack` had stopped printing the canary, but explicit `dctx map read m:.env` still returned the file. Trail-Code and graphify leaked nothing in that run. |

## Run 7: 140 of 140 (main `53f8b6b`, 31 October, 06:20 UTC)

New since run 6:
- unresolved-call output: `neighbors --dir out` also lists the calls the index cannot resolve, as `calls:out:?<name>` records after the resolved callees. These are receiver methods, builtins and external package calls.
- dotted config keys: dotted config key matching (`dotted_key`), not yet wired into `find`.
- PowerShell edges: PowerShell symbols and command-position call edges.

All landed checks passed together on the Linux benchmark host before the run. Raw results are in `research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks/results/run5-53f8b6b/` and `research/bench-3way-20261030/results/run7-53f8b6b/`.

**Task-level protocol** (70 questions, 354 gold facts; generator, mapping and scorer unchanged):

| Tool | Points /140 | Gold facts /354 | Tokens | Facts per 1k tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dctx `53f8b6b` | **140** (run 6: 136) | **353** (342) | **29,340** | **12.0** |
| Trail-Code 0.28.0 | 122 | 312 | 88,923 | 3.51 |
| graphify 0.9.97, code-only | 96 | 238 | 197,203 | 1.21 |

dctx scores every point on all ten question types. Callees went from 10 to 14 of 14 (37 of 38 facts). It uses a third of Trail-Code's tokens and a seventh of graphify's.

**Three-way run 7**: callers P / R on the first page 0.995 / 0.851 (all pages 0.968), the same as run 6. The language coverage table is unchanged at 10 of 10 with symbols and 9 of 10 with call edges; shell is still `n`. Its per-language edge counts rise (for example Scala 1 to 8) because the probe counts every `calls` record, and the new unresolved-call output includes the `calls:out:?` names. A count above zero says nothing new about resolved edges, so this run does not claim more resolved edges.

## Run 6 (main `82ec474`, 31 October, 02:04 UTC)

New since run 5:
- declaration-definition pairing: a declaration-only symbol (`.mli`, C/C++ header, `.d.ts`) answers neighbors for its paired definition.
- Erlang support: Erlang (not in the mixed corpus).
- export-list extraction and outgoing-call extraction: `export_list` and `out_calls`, which are not yet wired into answers.

All landed checks plus these four passed together on the Linux benchmark host before the run. Raw results are in `research/bench-3way-20261030/results/run6-82ec474/` and `research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks/results/run4-82ec474/`.

- Call-edge coverage on the mixed corpus: **9 of 10** (run 5: 8). OCaml now has edges through the `.mli` pairing. Shell still has none, because the probe samples bats `@test` blocks that call only external commands. Trail-Code has 7 and graphify 5.
- Callers P / R, first page: 0.995 / 0.851, unchanged (all pages 0.968).
- Task protocol: **136 / 140**, unchanged. Trail-Code has 122 and graphify 96. The 4 lost points are still callees questions; the next unresolved-call output improvement wires `out_calls` into neighbors.

## Latest: run 5 and task-level re-run 3 (main `a906884`, 30 October, 16:39 and 17:05 UTC)

dctx `a906884` adds four improvements on top of run 4. Caller-diversity improvements spread callers over files, makes bare calls skip methods, and ranks data-file keys below code. Declaration ranking puts exported declarations first in outlines, gives read sites for config keys, adds line numbers to find, and ranks exact-word concepts first. Caller paging orders callers by call-site count and fits pages to the budget. Language outline improvements add deeper Scala, Zig, Lua, Elixir and OCaml symbols. All 36 landed checks passed together on the Linux benchmark host before the run. The binary's sha256 starts with `76d8e9b59821`. Raw results are in `research/bench-3way-20261030/results/run5-a906884/` and `research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks/results/run3-a906884/`.

| graphify 0.9.97, code-only | 96 | 238 | 197,203 | 1.21 |

| concept | **14** | 12 | 10 |

dctx leads or ties on every type. The 4 points it still loses are all callees questions: ripgrep, pocketbase, django and core lose 1 each. In the three public corpora every missing fact is a call that the index could not resolve: a receiver method (`line_terminator`, `lookup_allowed`), a builtin (`callable`) or an external package (`Validate`). The core rows are sanitized. Unresolved-call reporting exposes these calls.

**Three-way run 5** (the same harness as runs 1-4):

Call-edge coverage on the mixed corpus is **8 of 10** by the probe; Trail-Code has 7 and graphify 5. The probe samples the first 25 symbols of the six largest files per language. - OCaml: the first 25 symbols all come from `cmdliner.mli`, an interface file with no bodies. On `cmdliner_arg.ml` itself, `str_of_pp` lists 3 callers with their call lines. Declaration-definition pairing makes an interface declaration answer for its definition.
- Shell: the first 25 symbols are bats `@test` blocks in `test/bats.bats`, which call external commands only.

| flask | skeleton | 44 ms, 866 | 991 ms, 852 | 514 ms, 474 |
| flask | overview | 45 ms, 491 | 1,009 ms, 1,122 | 7 ms, 5,930 |
| pocketbase | search | 213 ms, 259 | 1,573 ms, 358 | 1,393 ms, 97 (exit 3) |
| pocketbase | callers | 214 ms, 464 | 1,195 ms, 175 | 777 ms, 24 |
| pocketbase | overview | 226 ms, 652 | 1,232 ms, 1,514 | 8 ms, 11,591 |
| trailcode | callers | 200 ms, 472 | 1,180 ms, 1,064 | 715 ms, 196 |
| trailcode | overview | 195 ms, 500 | 1,159 ms, 499 | 7 ms, 10,076 |

All corpora and the edit-stability, network and coverage tables are in
[`research/bench-3way-20261030/results/headline.md`](research/bench-3way-20261030/results/headline.md).

## Method

- Host: a Linux benchmark host (Debian 13, Xeon E5-2680 v2), shared with other jobs. Load was 3.2 at the start, so absolute
  latencies are noisy. Every measured command ran as `nice -n 10 taskset -c 24-31 unshare -Urn env -i …`, with no
  network, scratch HOME and caches, and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`. One heavy process ran at a time. The network audit is a
  ptrace socket tracer, because strace is not installed.
- Corpora are pinned by SHA in `research/bench-3way-20261030/corpora-shas.json`: flask 3.1.3, ripgrep 15.2.0,
  pocketbase v0.40.5, Trail-Code at the 0.28.0 release commit, a mixed corpus of one public repo for each of 10
  languages, and a docs corpus built from python/devguide, rust-lang/book and asciidoctor.
- Tokens are `ceil(stdout_bytes / 3.5)` for every tool. That is an estimate, not a tokenizer.
- Cold runs use 3 repetitions, except 1 for any tool whose first run took more than 30 s (Trail-Code and graphify
  on pocketbase and trailcode). Warm runs take the median of 5 after one discarded warm-up.
- The callers gold set is the regex oracle of the October protocol (`goldlib.py`) on 20 seeded targets per corpus.
  A hit is true when its span contains a gold call site.
- Query mapping: dctx `map find` / `map neighbors --dir in --edge calls` / `map skeleton` / `map hubs`.
  Trail-Code `ask` / `callers` / `skeleton` / `map`. graphify `query` / `affected --relation calls` /
  `explain <file>` / `GRAPH_REPORT.md`.

## Not claimed

These exclusions apply to the historical tool-output protocols below the whole-session summary above.

- Whole-session cost or task-level answer quality from these historical protocols. Historical fact scores describe raw tool outputs only; the [11 November study](BENCHMARK-20261111.md) measures whole sessions with a frozen model.
- Anything about graphify's LLM semantic graph, or Trail-Code's learnings and LSP edges.
- SWE-bench scores or agent-run numbers from these historical tool-output protocols.
- Equal language depth. dctx's 25 new formats are outline tier: symbols, not call edges.

## Changes included in the October baseline

Call and import edges (`19e90a1`), byte-stable answers (`ce18608`), `.env` omission in pack (`6d4deec`),
outline symbols for 25 formats and plain-text sections (`9c61ac9`, `e0821e3`, `839bd45`, `a32dad3`),
neighbors depth 4 (`0de5ce1`), `hubs` (`6bc0cbc`), `grep` (`5691234`), `skeleton` (`2243c38`), `path` (`670e9e3`),
`export` (`ac8408c`), `dctx mcp` (`50bbce4`) and a 1 GiB source ceiling (`5d26781`). Each feature's focused check, and
then all 15 checks together on `ac8408c`, passed on the Linux benchmark host before the benchmark ran.

## Next

1. sensitive-file read protection: map mode must never serve env-shaped files. This is the remaining privacy leak.
2. Call edges for the outline tier, to close the 0-of-10 call-edge coverage on the mixed corpus.
3. Recall on ripgrep and trailcode (0.25 and 0.33 against Trail-Code's 0.33 and 0.90): method calls through
   receivers and re-exports.
4. Re-run the 70-question task protocol with a frozen model.

## Independent benchmark, 31.10.2026, run uncapped on the Linux benchmark host

Seeded selection of 3 repos the tools never saw (zoxide, requests, gin), gold from language servers and repo history, published regardless of outcome. Tasks: dctx 22/28 points, 31/36 facts, 6.85 facts per 1k tokens (Trail-Code 19/28, graphify 14/28). Callers against LSP gold, first page: dctx P 0.730 / R 0.341, Trail-Code P 0.731 / R 0.313, graphify P 0.920 / R 0.264. Honest read: dctx leads on task answers and token efficiency; caller recall on unseen repos is far below the in-house corpus (0.851), so the caller floors above hold only for the curated corpora. Full table and raw JSON: `docs/research/bench-independent/results/20261031T191225Z/`.

# CLI exit codes

`dctx map`, `dctx pack`, `dctx context`, `dctx doctor`, `dctx rpc`, `dctx mcp`, `dctx languages`, `dctx cache`, `dctx template`, a bare `dctx` without a terminal, an unknown command and a non-UTF-8 argument follow one contract:

`dctx serve [PATH]` and `dctx serve --mcp [PATH]` are aliases for `dctx mcp [PATH]`.
They use the current directory when PATH is omitted, including a directory named
`fixtures`; tools index paths relative to that directory. `dctx read` is an alias
for `dctx map read`, with the same flags and exit codes.

| Code | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ok: the command answered | a `find` page, including one with no hits; `--help` |
| 1 | no result: the command ran, but the named target or input has no answer | `map read m:nope.py` (an id not in the index); `map read logo.png` (a binary file); `pack` of a directory with no packable file |
| 2 | usage: the arguments are wrong | an unknown command or flag; a missing target (`dctx context` with no TARGET); `--depth 9`; an empty `find` query; a stale `--cursor`; `m:../outside`; a non-UTF-8 argument; `cache purge` without `--root`/`--all` or `--yes`; a template that does not compile; a bare `dctx` whose stdin or stdout is not a terminal |
| 3 | index error: the place, source, cache or index could not be opened, read, built or written | `--place /no/such/dir`; a corrupt or busy cache; a source over `DCTX_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES`; an `--output` file that cannot be written; `template build /no/such/file` (the message names the path) |

Every failure prints two lines on stderr: `[no] Error: <what went wrong>` (prefixed with the command, as `map: …`), then `hint: <what to do next>`. No input should reach a Rust panic; `crates/dctx-cli/tests/cli_errors.rs` and `<repo>/scripts/checks/V1-5.zsh` run twelve bad inputs and assert the code, the message, the hint and the absence of `panicked`.

## Details

- An id the index does not hold is a facade outcome (`gone`), not an error. `dctx map` prints the `gone` page on stdout, then exits 1 with the hint. `dctx mcp` returns the same page to the client as a normal tool result.
- An empty `find` or `grep` page is an answer and exits 0. Exit 1 is for a named target that is not there.
- A binary target is detected before the scan: a NUL byte in the first 8 KiB of the file named by `map`, `skeleton`, `explain` or `read` (path or `m:` id). `neighbors` and `path` still accept such a module, since source files can import it.
- `dctx pack` exits 1 only when no view filter is set (`--ext`, `--include`, `--exclude`, `--binary`, `--empty`, `--non-empty`, `--large`, `--small`, `--hidden`, `--debug-ignored`). A filter that matches nothing still prints an empty page and exits 0. The page (stdout) and the `pack bytes=…` status line (stderr) are printed before the exit-1 message. `pack` exit 3 covers source, scan, render and output failures.
- A reader that closes stdout early (`dctx pack . | head -1`) ends the run with exit 0 and no message, as `cat` does; every other failure keeps its code.
- `dctx pack --for <TEXT>` exits 1 when no name in TEXT matched the index (the page is printed first), 2 for a bad flag or a `--budget` outside 100..100000 (or `--budget` without `--for`), and 3 when PATH is not a directory or the index fails.
- `dctx mcp [--profile default|lean|three | --tools NAME,...] [PATH]` exits 3 when PATH cannot be entered and 2 for invalid arguments (including unknown tool names/profiles). See the [MCP guide](guides/MCP.md). Once serving, a failed tool call goes back to the client as a result with `isError: true`; unknown or unselected tools return JSON-RPC `-32602`. The server exits 0 at end of input.
- A facade refusal of the query (`InvalidRequest`, `BudgetTooSmall`, `StaleContinuation`, `Stale`, `UnsupportedCapability`, `UnsupportedVersion`) is 2; `PolicyDenied` and `PolicyUnavailable` are 1; every other facade error, and every error of the snapshot build, is 3. The mapping is `dctx_cli::exit::from_facade`.
- `map hubs`, `map path` and `map export` report their facade errors as text: an `unknown id` end of `map path` is 1, anything else 3.
- `dctx context` with no TARGET is 2; `dctx context --help` prints usage and exits 0. A TARGET that names nothing prints its empty page, then exits 1.
- `dctx cache` exits 2 for a bad flag or value, a purge without `--root PATH`/`--all` or `--yes`, and a `--max-bytes` that would loosen the cap; 1 for a `--root` id the ledger does not hold; 3 when the cache directory, policy or ledger cannot be read or written (the message names the directory).
- `dctx template` exits 2 for a bad flag and for a template that does not compile, and 3 when the template, the `--dir` directory or the `--output` file cannot be read or written (the message names the path). `--output` never writes through a symbolic link and refuses a target that is not a regular file.
- `dctx` with no command opens the interactive menu only when stdin and stdout are terminals; otherwise it prints the short usage as a hint and exits 2.
- `dctx doctor` follows the contract; `dctx rpc` keeps exit 0 at end of input (see Engine RPC below).

## Outside the contract

`dctx plugin …` and `dctx git …` return the plugin host's own codes.

## Engine RPC

`dctx rpc` uses the same operation paths and numeric taxonomy over
[versioned NDJSON](protocol/README.md). Each reply carries `engine_version`
and echoes its request id. An error contains the CLI code, diagnostic, hint and
any stdout emitted before failure (including gone pages). Protocol/framing
refusals use code 2 and leave the session usable. Cache status replies carry
the same codes and hints as `dctx cache status`. An error reply does not change the server's process exit
status: normal EOF exits 0, transport I/O errors exit 3, and broken stdout exits
quietly with 0. The server performs no piggyback auto-clean.

`pack --for TEXT --json` now emits the facade's context JSON page; its text
member contains the same budgeted context page as plain `pack --for TEXT`.

</FILE_CONTENT_END ID="F018">

# Crate map

Static checkout guide for contributors and coding assistants.
40 non-fixture Cargo packages: 36 under `crates/`, one plugin, one desktop,
and two standalone tools. Root `Cargo.toml` includes crates, plugins and desktop;
each tool declares its own workspace. `bindings/README.md` describes planned
bindings; root membership for Python/Node is commented out. Fixture manifests
under tests are not product crates.

## How to read the inventory

Each row gives purpose, layer, direct first-party path dependencies, and direct
external **normal** dependencies. `none` means std-only at that crate boundary;
`first-party only` means no direct external normal dependency, not an assertion
about the complete dependency closure. Dev/build dependencies are excluded.
Optional and target-specific normal dependencies are explicitly marked.
Resolved transitive dependencies and runtime behavior are **unverified** here.

Source convention: for every row named `X`, purpose is taken from
`crates/X/src/lib.rs:1` (first six lines), and dependency names from
`crates/X/Cargo.toml` `[dependencies]`. These two paths are the row's evidence.
Exceptions use the directory shown in the row. Desktop purpose comes from
`apps/dctx-desktop/README.md:3`; its lib header has no purpose description.
Layer labels are navigation classifications of those headers, using the accepted
boundaries in `docs/design/ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md` (DX-ARCH-01).

## Shipped CLI path (v1)

What the `dctx` binary (`crates/dctx-cli`) actually runs, as of v1. No refactor: the other crates stay in the workspace.

- **Shipped:** `dctx-cli` and the `crates/dctx` facade session (index, find, grep, callers, callees, neighbors, skeleton, hubs, pack, read), with dctx-core (selection), dctx-hash, dctx-ports, dctx-pack, dctx-template, dctx-adapter-cache, dctx-adapter-fs (compatibility IO), dctx-map-model (records and rendering) and the `dctx-lex-*` extractors.
- **Request types only:** `dctx-map-query`. The CLI imports `Request`, `Verb`, `Direction`, `Format`, `AnswerBudget` and `EdgeKind`; its `Index` engine is never called.
- **Internal or legacy (compiled as dependencies of `dctx-map-query`, not run by the CLI):** the `dctx-map-query` `Index` engine, `dctx-map-store`, `dctx-map-scan`, `dctx-map-resolve`, `dctx-map-segment`, `dctx-adapter-store`; `dctx-map-parse` likewise. docs/SPEC-MAP-MODE.md sections 6–8 and 10 describe this engine.
- **Unstable (no stability promise in v1):** dctx-plugin-host, dctx-plugin-platform, dctx-plugin-protocol, dctx-plugin-distribution and dctx-desktop-api. The default `dctx-cli` build enables the plugin runtime and the bundled Git plugin process; `--no-default-features --features strict` builds without them.

## Core, engines and adapters

| Crate | Purpose from header | Layer | Direct path dependencies | Direct external normal dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dctx-hash | First-party SHA-256 content digests. | pure core | none | none (std-only) |
| dctx-core | Pure domain: ids, selection decisions, budgets, errors, pack facts and settings parsing. | pure core | dctx-hash | first-party only |
| dctx-ports | Boundary traits Source, FactStore, Cache, Clock, Cancellation; in-memory implementations and spies. | pure core | dctx-core | first-party only |
| dctx-map-model | IO-free map identities, byte spans, precision, provenance and answers. | pure core | dctx-hash | serde, serde_json (optional `wire-json`, enabled by default) |
| dctx-map-segment | Pure safe codec for immutable map index segments. | pure core | dctx-hash | thiserror |
| dctx-template | Pure DTS v1 renderer and v2 ContextPlan compiler. | mode engine | dctx-core, dctx-hash | first-party only |
| dctx-pack | Pack snapshot and diff engine over injected ports, with no concrete IO. | mode engine | dctx-core, dctx-hash, dctx-ports | first-party only |
| dctx-map-scan | Model-independent scan privacy rules. | mode engine | none | sha2, thiserror |
| dctx-map-parse | Per-file syntax facts; PureParser over lexers, optional tree-sitter oracle. | lexer/parser | dctx-map-model, dctx-lex-rust, dctx-lex-js, dctx-lex-md, dctx-lex-py, dctx-lex-go, dctx-lex-java, dctx-lex-c, dctx-lex-cfg, dctx-lex-cs, dctx-lex-kt, dctx-lex-rb, dctx-lex-php, dctx-lex-swift | sha2, thiserror; optional: tree-sitter, tree-sitter-rust, tree-sitter-md, tree-sitter-javascript, tree-sitter-typescript (`syntax-tree-sitter`) |
| dctx-map-resolve | Pure symbol resolution and move detection. | mode engine | dctx-map-model | thiserror |
| dctx-map-store | Persistent graph facts, pack snapshots and content-addressed comparison cache. | adapter | dctx-core, dctx-hash, dctx-map-model, dctx-ports | rusqlite (`bundled`), thiserror, serde_json |
| dctx-map-query | Incremental indexing and bounded traversal; wires scan, parse, resolve and store APIs. | mode engine | dctx-map-model, dctx-map-scan, dctx-map-parse, dctx-map-resolve, dctx-map-store, dctx-map-segment, dctx-ports, dctx-adapter-fs, dctx-adapter-store, dctx-adapter-cache, dctx-core, dctx-hash | thiserror, serde, serde_json |
| dctx-adapter-fs | Confined filesystem Source adapter; selection before content. | adapter | dctx-hash | thiserror |
| dctx-adapter-store | Filesystem publication of immutable map segments and manifest generations. | adapter | dctx-hash, dctx-map-segment | thiserror |
| dctx-adapter-cache | Cache quotas, leases, expiry, persisted ledger and bounded auto-clean. | adapter | dctx-core, dctx-hash, dctx-ports | thiserror |

## Lexers and structural extractors

Purpose below retains the language and extractor role from each lib header.
Several headers say “zero-dependency”; manifests qualify that statement: the
model-dependent lexers have first-party direct dependencies, and
`dctx-map-model` defaults to external JSON dependencies. Do not infer an
external-free closure from the header wording.

| Crate | Purpose from header | Layer | Direct path dependencies | Direct external normal dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dctx-lex-rust | Structural Rust extractor built on syn. | lexer/parser | none | proc-macro2, quote, syn, thiserror |
| dctx-lex-js | Hand-written JavaScript and TypeScript structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-md | Hand-written Markdown structure extractor. | lexer/parser | none | none (std-only) |
| dctx-lex-py | Hand-written Python structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-go | Hand-written Go structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-java | Hand-written Java structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-c | Hand-written C and C++ structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-cfg | Hand-written configuration structural extractor (JSON, TOML, YAML). | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-cs | Hand-written C# structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-kt | Hand-written Kotlin structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-rb | Hand-written Ruby structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |
| dctx-lex-php | Hand-written PHP structural extractor. | lexer/parser | dctx-hash, dctx-map-model | first-party only |

## Plugin infrastructure, facade and surfaces

| Crate | Purpose from header | Layer | Direct path dependencies | Direct external normal dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dctx-ed25519 | Ed25519 verification for plugin trust, via audited ed25519-dalek. | pure core | none | ed25519-dalek |
| dctx-plugin-protocol | Std-only codec and typed records for frozen plugin API v1. | plugin | none | none (std-only) |
| dctx-plugin-host | Plugin host domain and brokers; authority, receipts, resources, lifecycle and hooks. | plugin | dctx-hash, dctx-plugin-protocol | first-party only |
| dctx-plugin-platform | Native plugin admission and platform security primitives; general native launches fail closed. | adapter | dctx-hash, dctx-plugin-protocol | thiserror; Linux-only: rustix, landlock, seccompiler (target dependency section) |
| dctx-plugin-distribution | Plugin installer, trust and discovery client: signed manifests, offline bundles, atomic activation. | plugin | dctx-ed25519, dctx-hash, dctx-plugin-protocol | first-party only |
| dctx-plugin-git (`plugins/dctx-plugin-git/`) | Bundled git plugin: local .gitignore protection and brokered git add .gitignore. | plugin | dctx-plugin-protocol | first-party only |
| dctx | Stable library facade for pack, map, templates, cache and optional plugin host. | facade | dctx-adapter-cache, dctx-core, dctx-hash, dctx-lex-js, dctx-lex-md, dctx-map-model, dctx-pack, dctx-ports, dctx-template; optional: dctx-lex-rust, dctx-plugin-host, dctx-plugin-platform, dctx-plugin-protocol | first-party only |
| dctx-cli | Library surface for cache administration; dctx binary wires the same modules. | surface | dctx, dctx-adapter-cache, dctx-core, dctx-map-query, dctx-plugin-distribution, dctx-plugin-protocol, dctx-template; optional: dctx-plugin-git | first-party only |
| dctx-desktop-api | Desktop engine seam for snapshots, settings, recent projects and plugin management. | surface | dctx, dctx-plugin-distribution, dctx-template | serde, serde_json |
| dctx-desktop (`apps/dctx-desktop/src-tauri/`) | Cross-platform GUI for dctx — Directory Context Generator (app README). | surface | dctx-desktop-api, dctx-plugin-distribution, dctx-plugin-protocol | tauri, tauri-plugin-shell, tauri-plugin-dialog, tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager, serde, serde_json, tokio, chrono, dirs |
| architecture-bench (`tools/architecture-bench/`) | Baseline for current dctx map mode. | tool | dctx-map-query | serde, serde_json, sha2, thiserror |
| plugin-index (`tools/plugin-index/`) | Local public-index validator for plugins. | tool | dctx-ed25519, dctx-hash | thiserror |

Tool purpose evidence: each tool's `src/lib.rs:1`; dependencies: its Cargo.toml.
Plugin purpose evidence: `plugins/dctx-plugin-git/src/lib.rs:1`.
Desktop dependencies: `apps/dctx-desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml`.
`tauri-build` is a desktop **build** dependency, outside the normal-dependency
columns. Linux plugin dependencies are the one target-specific addition above.
The facade does not directly depend on dctx-map-query: do not turn an intended
architectural boundary into an invented Cargo edge. Its optional Rust extractor
uses `syntax-rust`; plugin runtime dependencies use `plugin-runtime`.

## Dependency picture: core toward consumers

This is a selected-edge tree, not an exhaustive DAG. Children consume parents;
repeated nodes have other inputs listed in the inventory. Every edge shown is
a direct path dependency in the child's manifest. Braces group sibling crates.

```text
dctx-hash
|-- dctx-core
|   |-- dctx-ports
|   |   `-- dctx-pack
|   |       `-- dctx
|   |           |-- dctx-cli
|   |           `-- dctx-desktop-api
|   |               `-- dctx-desktop
|   `-- dctx-template --> {dctx, dctx-cli, dctx-desktop-api}
|-- dctx-map-model
|   |-- dctx-lex-{js,py,go,java,c,cfg,cs,kt,rb,php,swift}
|   |   `-- dctx-map-parse <-- {dctx-lex-rust, dctx-lex-md}
|   |       `-- dctx-map-query
|   |           |-- dctx-cli
|   |           `-- architecture-bench
|   |-- dctx-map-resolve --> dctx-map-query
|   `-- dctx-map-store --> dctx-map-query
|-- dctx-map-segment
|   `-- dctx-adapter-store --> dctx-map-query
|-- dctx-adapter-fs --> dctx-map-query
|-- dctx-adapter-cache --> {dctx, dctx-cli, dctx-map-query}
|-- dctx-plugin-host --> dctx [optional]
|-- dctx-plugin-platform --> dctx [optional]
|-- dctx-plugin-distribution --> {dctx-cli, dctx-desktop-api, dctx-desktop}
`-- plugin-index
dctx-map-scan --> dctx-map-query
dctx-ed25519 --> {dctx-plugin-distribution, plugin-index}
dctx-plugin-protocol
`-- {dctx-plugin-host, dctx-plugin-platform, dctx-plugin-distribution,
     dctx-plugin-git, dctx [optional], dctx-cli, dctx-desktop}
dctx-plugin-git --> dctx-cli [optional]
```

## Language wiring

Authoritative variants and extension selection:
`crates/dctx-map-parse/src/domain/facts.rs:8` (`Language`, `for_path`).
Dispatch: `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/mod.rs:40` (`PureParser`).
Adapter paths below are relative to `crates/dctx-map-parse/src/adapters/`;
each file imports the named lexer. These are all 13 `dctx-lex-*` packages.

| Language variant(s) | Lexer crate | Adapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | dctx-lex-rust | rust.rs |
| JavaScript, TypeScript, Tsx | dctx-lex-js | javascript.rs |
| Markdown | dctx-lex-md | markdown.rs |
| Python | dctx-lex-py | python.rs |
| Go | dctx-lex-go | go.rs |
| Java | dctx-lex-java | java.rs |
| C (C and C++) | dctx-lex-c | c.rs |
| Config (JSON/JSONC, TOML, YAML) | dctx-lex-cfg | config.rs |
| CSharp | dctx-lex-cs | csharp.rs |
| Kotlin | dctx-lex-kt | kotlin.rs |
| Ruby | dctx-lex-rb | ruby.rs |
| Php | dctx-lex-php | php.rs |
| Swift | dctx-lex-swift | swift.rs |
| Unknown | none | mod.rs fallback: module-only |

The optional `TreeSitterParser` in `adapters/mod.rs:74` uses grammars for Rust,
JavaScript/TypeScript/Tsx and Markdown. Other known languages take the pure
adapters; Unknown takes fallback. This is an oracle feature, not the default.

## Cross-cutting rules and evidence locations

- **No Git in the core:** [product contracts](design/PRODUCT-CONTRACTS.md)
  records the core ban and plain-text .gitignore exception. Enforcement evidence:
  `crates/dctx-map-query/tests/no_git.rs` (source spawn audit, PATH trap and
  source-port privacy tests). VCS effects belong to the plugin, not the core.
- **Privacy, selection before content:** `crates/dctx-adapter-fs/tests/privacy.rs`
  uses read spies to check ignored/omitted paths remain unopened;
  `crates/dctx-map-query/tests/source_privacy.rs` checks secrets, ignored files,
  traversal and symlinks, with an included-file positive control.
- **Pure domain boundary:** `crates/dctx-core/src/lib.rs:1` points to
  `crates/dctx-core/tests/purity.rs`, which checks every source module without a
  directory exemption. Comments and unit-test tails are excluded from the IO scan.
  The crate retains its first-party dctx-hash dependency.
- **Plugin PP1–PP10:** [historical PP matrix](archive/design/plugin-evidence/PP-MATRIX.md) maps tests,
  formal evidence and gaps: PP1 authority narrows; PP2 excluded-source privacy;
  PP3 effect audit; PP4 protocol binding; PP5 no blind replay; PP6 strict isolation;
  PP7 bounded resources; PP8 lifecycle progress; PP9 install integrity;
  PP10 hook order/result truth. The matrix is dated scout evidence, not a fresh
  passing test result or certification of today's product acceptance.
- **Legacy removal:** The migration removed the core IO wrappers and their exports.
  [legacy removal inventory](archive/design/D3-LEGACY-REMOVAL.md) remains the historical inventory;
  [compatibility record](archive/design/D3-COMPATIBILITY.md) maps retired families to retained tests.
  Pack codecs, template rendering, filesystem adapters and CLI compatibility IO
  own the replacements. Pure core modules, settings and template assets remain.

## Validation commands

Use [TESTING.md](TESTING.md) for the current commands, toolchains, matrix and
exclusions. Desktop backend checks use `tools/desktop-check.sh`; browser evidence
uses `bun run e2e` from `apps/dctx-desktop`. A skipped desktop check does not
qualify a desktop release. Standalone tools have their own workspaces and checks.

</FILE_CONTENT_END ID="F019">
<FILE_CONTENT_START ID="F020" PATH="docs/MODALITIES.md" LINES="340">
